Embracing British Rain

If you wait for dry weather to tour the UK, you will never leave your garage. Rain is an inevitable companion on British motorcycle tours and the riders who enjoy touring most are those who have mastered the art of staying dry. A comprehensive rain gear strategy means you can ride all day in the wet and still arrive at your destination comfortable and smiling.

The Layered Approach to Rain Protection

Rather than relying on a single piece of gear, the best rain protection uses multiple complementary layers:

  • Waterproof outer jacket and trousers — Your primary defence. Laminated construction is best for sustained rain.
  • Waterproof boots — Gore-Tex lined boots keep feet dry where water exposure is constant.
  • Waterproof gloves — Membrane gloves or rain over-gloves protect hands from cold, wet misery.
  • Neck seal — A neoprene or waterproof neck gaiter prevents rain running down inside your jacket collar.
  • Waterproof oversuit — For riders whose primary gear is not fully waterproof, a packable oversuit provides emergency rain protection.

Best Rain Gear for Touring

Oxford Rainseal Oversuit — One-piece oversuit that goes over your riding gear. Quick to put on at the roadside with a simple zip. Compact enough to live permanently in a pannier.

Rev It Pacific 3 H2O — Separate waterproof jacket and trousers that pack down small. Reflective details improve visibility in the rain and the fit accommodates your riding gear beneath.

Held Rainstretch — Stretchy waterproof overtrousers that pull on over boots and riding trousers. The stretch material makes them easy to deploy at the roadside without removing boots.

SealSkinz Waterproof Socks — Worn inside your boots as an additional waterproof layer. Excellent insurance if your boot membrane eventually fails.

Never pack your rain gear at the bottom of a pannier. It needs to be instantly accessible when the first drops fall. Keep your oversuit in a tank bag or the top of a pannier where you can grab it in seconds.

Riding Technique in Rain

Beyond gear, adjust your riding for wet conditions. Increase following distances, brake earlier and more gently, avoid painted road markings and manhole covers which become treacherous when wet, and be particularly cautious in the first 30 minutes of rain when road oils lift to the surface. Smooth inputs to throttle, brakes, and steering are the key to safe wet-weather riding.

Drying Gear on Tour

Drying wet gear overnight at accommodation is an essential touring skill. Hang wet items over radiators or shower rails with newspaper underneath to catch drips. Boot dryers are compact enough to pack and invaluable for drying waterproof boots overnight. Many motorcycling-friendly hotels offer a drying room if you ask politely.
keyTakeaways: A layered approach beats any single item: waterproof outer, boots, gloves and a neck seal.
Keep a packable oversuit accessible in a tank bag, never buried at the bottom of a pannier.
Laminated waterproof construction copes best with sustained British rain.
The first 30 minutes of rain are the most treacherous as road oils lift to the surface.
A neck gaiter stops rain running down inside your collar and soaking your base layers.

comparisonTable.caption: Rain gear options for UK touring

pros: Layering lets you adapt to changing weather through the day.
A packable oversuit deploys in seconds when the first drops fall.
Staying dry prevents heat loss that impairs concentration and reactions.
cons: Oversuits can flap in the wind and are awkward to don at speed.
Cheaper drop-liner gear soaks up water and becomes heavy.
Drying gear overnight on tour takes planning and radiator space.

faq.q: Should I buy a waterproof jacket or an oversuit?
faq.a: Both have a place. A laminated waterproof jacket and trousers are the best primary defence for sustained rain, as the membrane keeps the outer shell from soaking up water. An oversuit is a lightweight overlayer worn on top of non-waterproof gear, which is cheap and packs small but flaps in the wind. Many riders use waterproof primary gear and still carry an oversuit as backup.

faq.q: Where should I keep my rain gear on tour?
faq.a: Never at the bottom of a pannier. Rain gear needs to be instantly accessible when the first drops fall, so keep your oversuit or waterproofs in a tank bag or at the very top of a pannier where you can grab it in seconds. Getting caught out and soaked because your waterproofs were buried is a miserable and avoidable mistake.

faq.q: How do I ride safely in the rain?
faq.a: Increase your following distances, brake earlier and more gently, and avoid painted road markings and manhole covers which become slippery when wet. Be especially cautious in the first 30 minutes of rain, when road oils lift to the surface and grip is at its worst. Smooth inputs to the throttle, brakes and steering are the key to safe wet-weather riding.

faq.q: How do I dry wet gear overnight?
faq.a: Hang wet items over radiators or a shower rail with newspaper underneath to catch drips. Boot dryers with gentle warm air are compact enough to pack and invaluable for drying waterproof boots. Many motorcycle-friendly hotels and B&Bs have a drying room if you ask politely, which is worth checking when you book accommodation for a wet tour.

faq.q: Do I need a waterproof neck seal?
faq.a: It makes a big difference. Rain runs down your helmet and straight inside an open collar, soaking your base layers no matter how good your jacket is. A neoprene or waterproof neck gaiter seals that gap, keeping your chest and back dry. It is a cheap, small item that transforms comfort on a long wet day in the saddle.
